# Changelog

## 0.2

- Read the authentications a Gen2 Super Sniffer card captured from a reader, and append them to the MFKey nonce log so MFKey can recover the keys. The card does the capturing; the arithmetic belongs to MFKey, which already implements it with the memory tricks the hardware needs and already writes what it finds into the user dictionary
- Set the sniffer card's UID, which Proxmark3 cannot: `hf mf supercard -u` answers "Not supported on this card" for Gen2, and `hf mf gen3uid` fails on it too. The sequence is five READ commands that mean nothing as reads (`30 F3`, `30 2A`, `30 BD`, `30 EF`, `30 01`), then one command per UID byte, seven of them, zero-padding a 4-byte UID
- Commit the write with HLTA. This is the step that makes it stick, and it is in no decompiled source: the vendor's Android app ends at its seventh byte and never halts, because the Android NFC stack sends HLTA below it on teardown. A wire trace shows the card *answering* that halt, which an ISO14443-3A tag never does, with its status byte going `11` to `22`; the next WUPA gets silence while it writes, and the one after returns the new UID. Without it the card acknowledges all twelve commands and discards the lot when the field drops
- Read the UID back off the card before calling a write a success, by cycling the field rather than halting it. A second HLTA would leave the card answering only WUPA while the firmware activates with REQA alone, so it would never come back; `NfcCommandReset` takes the field down for 100 ms instead, which powers the card out of whatever state the write left it in. A few activations are spent waiting, because a card busy writing answers nothing
- Take the UID to write from a tag, from a saved `.nfc` dump, or typed in by hand. The card whose keys are wanted is not always the one in reach
- Refuse a UID of a different length from the sniffer card's own, naming both lengths. These cards are physically a 4-byte or a 7-byte part and cannot be made into the other, so the only useful thing to say is which one you are holding and which one you picked
- Pair captures exhaustively rather than one pair per key, reversing the first version's greedy pairing. A card read during development disproved the assumption it rested on: seven captures, all sector 0, and not one of the nine possible pairings recovered a key, because the reader had presented a different key each time. Which captures share a key is what mfkey32 answers, not something that can be decided beforehand. Proxmark3 pairs exhaustively for the same reason - it can afford to, finishing in milliseconds where MFKey takes minutes a line, so the cost here lands on the user's time
- Pair only captures from the same card. mfkey32 seeds the cipher with the UID, so a pair spanning two of them is arithmetically impossible however well its sector and key type match. One read can hold both: these cards keep older captures when a new one lands, so reprogramming the UID between taps leaves two UIDs on one card
- Skip a pair the log already holds, all six words of it, either way round. These cards keep their captures until a reader overwrites them, so reading one twice is an ordinary thing to do - and MFKey does not deduplicate, running the full attack per line and only consulting the dictionaries for keys it has already found
- Show the captures as a table: two bold lines for what came off the card and where that leaves the log, then sector, key type and tag nonce in the one monospaced font available. The nonce has to be there - a reader working one sector produces rows identical in everything else, and a reader trying several keys against that sector produces them with different keys behind them. The UID is a row of its own, printed when it changes, because every capture of one read normally shares it
- Offer to run MFKey when it is installed, the way the firmware's NFC app does after Detect Reader, and name qUnleashed either way: a pair takes minutes on the Flipper and seconds on a PC
- Tell a read that broke off from a card with nothing on it. A read that stopped early has left captures unread, and the advice for an empty card - go and tap a reader - would overwrite them, so the app's own misreading would be what destroyed them
- Identify the card passively. It is recognised by answering an unauthenticated `30 00` while presenting a MIFARE Classic SAK; a genuine Classic refuses that read, and an Ultralight answers it but cannot present that SAK. The vendor app has a stronger signature, `30 F3` answering `0x11`, but that byte is also the first step of the sequence that arms a UID write, and a read must not be able to change the card
- Say which kind of wrong card it is. "Does not answer an unauthenticated read" is false about an Ultralight - it does answer, which is why the SAK is tested first - and the two cases call for different cards
- Treat the nonce log as something that can fail. The stream caches about a kilobyte in RAM, so for a short run nothing reaches the SD card until it is closed; the close is now part of the result rather than cleanup, the lines are built whole and written once so a failure cannot leave a half-written line in a file MFKey parses without validating, and the `nfc` folder is created first as the firmware's own NFC app does
- Explain the job in order under How to Use, rather than describing the app. Someone opening it has a card in one hand and does not know which menu entry comes first

## 0.1

- Initial read-only version: read a Gen2 card's trace slots with plain `30 00`..`30 07` and write the captures out as MFKey32 nonces
- Judge each slot on its contents rather than its index - the command byte has to be one a reader would send, and a slot that captured nothing leaves the reader's two words zero. The vendor app reads eight slots and Proxmark3 reads seven, so neither count is a reason to truncate a card that uses the other
- Expand the stored tag nonce before writing it out. The card keeps `nt` as the 16-bit Crypto1 PRNG state rather than the nonce the reader saw, which loses nothing - the generator is a 16-bit LFSR - but has to be run forward 31 steps. Verified against the vendor app's own test vector: its two sample records, parsed at these offsets and expanded this way, recover `A0A1A2A3A4A5` through Proxmark3's `mfkey32v2`
- Pair captures by sector and key type rather than by block. One key covers every block in its sector and a reader walks a sector authenticating against whichever block it likes
- Append to `/ext/nfc/.mfkey32.log` in the firmware's own line format, byte for byte, so nonces sniffed off a reader with the Flipper and nonces lifted off a sniffer card accumulate in the same place. The format matters exactly: MFKey does not parse it with a format string, it walks space-separated tokens and keeps the 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 13th, 15th and 17th
